You need to provide more practice problems. Doing one example on the board is not enough for us to master complex equations.
Stop ignoring the students who raise their hands. If you are going to ask a question, you have to actually let us answer it.
Your lectures lack any sort of structure. An outline at the beginning of class would help us follow your train of thought.
Please stop making us buy a $200 access code just to submit our homework. It is a predatory practice and completely unfair.
You need to be more flexible with deadlines when students have documented medical emergencies. Life happens.
Stop using the phrase "as you should already know." If we already knew it, we wouldn't be taking this introductory class.
Your syllabus completely lacks an accessibility statement. You need to be more proactive about supporting students with accommodations.
Please stop giving pop quizzes. They don't measure learning; they just create unnecessary anxiety and stress for the students.
reviews.rating_tags: Tough grader--Beware of pop quizzes--Lecture heavy

reviews.comment: You need to learn how to use the classroom technology. We waste ten minutes every day watching you struggle with the projector.
Stop canceling class at the last minute. We commute to campus specifically for this block, and it wastes our entire morning.
Your exams focus way too much on obscure trivia rather than the main concepts we spent weeks discussing in lecture.
You need to provide actual feedback, not just a letter grade. A "B-" tells me nothing about what I need to improve for next time.
Stop assigning group work in an asynchronous online class. Coordinating schedules across time zones is an absolute nightmare.
Your tone in emails is incredibly condescending. A simple question does not warrant a lecture on our supposed lack of effort.
Please stop using incredibly small fonts on your PowerPoint slides. We can't read 12-point font from thirty feet away.
You need to actually moderate the online discussion boards. Right now, it's just a free-for-all of incorrect information.
Stop making attendance mandatory if you are just going to read the textbook to us. We can do that at home.
Your instructions for the final project are entirely too vague. We need a clear outline of what you actually expect from us.
Please stop whispering. If you aren't going to use a microphone, you absolutely must project your voice to the back of the room.
reviews.rating_tags: Tough grader--Beware of pop quizzes--Lecture heavy

reviews.comment: You need to update your lecture materials. Some of your references and jokes are from the 1990s and completely land flat.
Stop playing favorites. It is obvious that you only call on the same three students and ignore the rest of the room.
Your grading curve makes no sense. Please explain the math behind how our final grades are actually calculated.
reviews.rating_tags: Tough grader--Beware of pop quizzes--Lecture heavy

reviews.comment: Please stop pacing so frantically while you lecture. It is incredibly distracting and makes it hard to focus on the material.
You need to provide study guides. Just telling us to "review your notes" is not helpful for a massive, cumulative final exam.
Stop assigning hundreds of pages of reading a week. It is physically impossible to keep up with, so nobody even tries anymore.
Your Canvas gradebook is a mess. Please organize it so we can actually calculate our current standing in the class.
Please stop ending class fifteen minutes late. We have other places to be, and holding us hostage is disrespectful of our time.
You need to connect the theories to real-world examples. Without practical application, this entire course feels pointless.
Stop relying on the textbook publisher's pre-made quizzes. They often cover material you explicitly told us to skip.
Please stop making sarcastic comments when a student gets an answer wrong. It discourages everyone from participating.
You need to actually grade the assignments before the midterm. We have no idea how we are doing in the class right now.
Stop posting the lecture slides as locked PDFs. We need to be able to highlight and annotate them during class.
reviews.rating_tags: Tough grader--Beware of pop quizzes--Lecture heavy

reviews.comment: Your multiple-choice questions are too tricky. They feel designed to trick us rather than actually test our knowledge.
Please stop changing the homework requirements the night before it's due. It is incredibly unfair to students who finish early.
reviews.rating_tags: Tough grader--Beware of pop quizzes--Lecture heavy

reviews.comment: You need to be more approachable. Students are terrified to ask questions because you always seem annoyed when we do.
Your syllabus is incredibly vague. We need actual due dates, not just "mid-October," so we can plan our semesters properly.
Stop assigning group projects where everyone gets the exact same grade regardless of individual effort. It rewards the slackers.
You need to reply to emails faster. Waiting five days for a response to a simple question is completely unacceptable.
Please stop going on political tangents. We are here to learn biology, not to listen to your personal opinions on the news.
Your feedback on essays is entirely illegible. If we can't read your handwriting, we can't learn from our mistakes.
reviews.rating_tags: Tough grader--Beware of pop quizzes--Lecture heavy

reviews.comment: Stop reading directly off your slides. We are all capable of reading. Use the class time to actually explain the concepts.
Your office hours are during the exact time most students have other classes. Please offer at least one alternate time slot.
The grading is far too subjective. We need a clear, standardized rubric so we understand exactly how we are being evaluated.
You need to speak much louder. Half the class is straining to hear your instructions and we are missing key information.
Stop assigning heavy reading that you never discuss in class. It feels like busywork and wastes our limited study time.
Please update your Canvas page. The current layout is a confusing maze and we can never find the assignments we need.
Your lectures would be much better if you actually looked at the students instead of staring at the back wall the entire time.
You need to create a culture where it's okay to admit you didn't understand the reading. If students are terrified to ask for clarification, no learning is actually happening.
Stop punishing the whole class because one person didn't do the reading. Giving a pop quiz to everyone just because nobody volunteered an answer is petty and vindictive.
You need to actually reference the readings in your exams. If we spent ten hours reading a novel, there should be at least one question about it on the midterm.
You need to provide a trigger warning for highly sensitive or graphic reading materials. Blindsiding students with traumatizing content is unacceptable in a modern classroom.
Stop changing the reading assignments at the last minute. Adding a 40-page article to the list the night before class is incredibly unfair to students who plan ahead.
You need to ensure the syllabus schedule matches the actual lectures. We are currently three weeks behind the syllabus, and nobody knows what we should be reading.
You need to provide reading questions to guide us. Handing us a 50-page article without telling us what themes or concepts we should be looking for is overwhelming.
Stop assigning 100 pages of reading a night. We are taking four other classes. A lighter, more focused reading load would result in much higher comprehension and engagement.
You need to make sure the textbook actually aligns with your personal teaching philosophy. If you disagree with everything in Chapter 4, just skip Chapter 4.
Please stop reading quotes directly from the textbook for twenty minutes straight. We can read the book ourselves. We need your analysis of the quotes, not an audiobook.
You need to summarize the key points of the reading before diving into a discussion. We all read it, but a quick refresher helps center the conversation.
You need to provide the reading materials as PDFs if they are out of print. Telling us to track down a rare book from 1985 to write an essay is entirely unreasonable.
You need to ensure the library has copies of the required texts on reserve. Not everyone can afford to drop $300 on books at the start of the semester.
Stop requiring us to buy supplementary books you wrote. It feels like a massive conflict of interest and a quick cash grab at the expense of your students.
You need to actively monitor the group dynamics. If a group is clearly dysfunctional, you need to step in and help mediate before the project completely falls apart.
You need to provide class time for group work. Expecting us to find three hours a week outside of class to meet up is completely unrealistic for commuter students.
Stop making group projects worth such a huge percentage of our grade. Our individual academic standing shouldn't be entirely dependent on the work ethic of strangers.
You need to assign group members rather than letting us pick. It prevents the same cliques from forming and forces us to learn how to work with different personalities.
Please stop making us do peer evaluations if you aren't going to actually read them. If the entire group says one person did nothing, that person shouldn't get an A.
You need to provide a clear outline of what each group member is responsible for. Vague group assignments always lead to one person doing 90% of the actual work.
Stop making the final project a group effort. By the end of the semester, everyone is burned out, and trying to coordinate a massive project is an absolute nightmare.
You need to be more lenient with bathroom breaks during a three-hour final. Forcing students to hold it or risk failing is a borderline human rights violation.
Please stop pacing up and down the aisles during exams. It is incredibly distracting and makes students feel like you are looking over their shoulders to judge them.
Stop refusing to answer questions during an exam. If a question is worded poorly, clarifying what it means is part of your job as an instructor.
You need to record your review sessions. The students who need the review the most are often the ones who are working during the times you schedule them.
You need to provide a study guide that actually reflects the exam content. A list of 500 vocabulary words is not a study guide; it's just the glossary of the textbook.
Stop putting questions on the exam that you explicitly said would not be on the exam. It destroys any trust the class has in your guidance.
You need to ensure your exams are free of typos. A misplaced decimal point in a math problem completely ruins the question and causes massive anxiety during the test.
Please stop writing questions that rely on double negatives. "Which of the following is not untrue" is completely unnecessary phrasing that just confuses students.
You need to provide a breakdown of the exam scores. Just posting the average isn't enough; we need to see the standard deviation to know how we actually performed.
Stop using multiple-choice questions where the choices are sentences that are entire paragraphs long. It tests our reading speed, not our knowledge of the subject.
You need to be more transparent about how the curve works. "I will apply a curve if necessary" is too vague. Tell us exactly what the mathematical formula will be.
Please stop making the midterm worth more than the final. It punishes students who took a few weeks to adjust to your teaching style but mastered the material by the end.
You need to slow down when speaking to students whose first language isn't English. Speaking louder doesn't help comprehension; speaking clearly and at a normal pace does.
You need to provide a clear path for contesting a grade. If we feel a TA graded us unfairly, there should be a formal, non-hostile way to appeal to you directly.
Please stop making assignments worth exactly one point. If we miss one tiny detail, we get a zero. Scale the assignments up so partial credit is actually possible.
You need to round up borderline grades. Refusing to bump an 89.9% to a 90% shows a severe lack of empathy and a rigid adherence to arbitrary numbers.
Stop using overly complicated grading formulas. If we need a spreadsheet to figure out what our current grade is, your system is entirely too complex.
You need to be more concise in your emails. A five-paragraph essay responding to a simple "where is the classroom" question is incredibly overwhelming to read.
Please stop canceling office hours at the last minute. When students have trekked across campus specifically to see you, an email sent ten minutes prior is unacceptable.
You need to actually hold a review session before the final. Just saying "come to office hours if you have questions" is not a substitute for a structured review.
Please stop sending mass emails that don't apply to the whole class. If it's an issue with one specific group, just email that group directly.
You need to update your syllabus to include a clear schedule of topics. "Subject to change" shouldn't mean we have no idea what we are learning next week.
You need to create a dedicated Q&A thread on Canvas. Having students email you the exact same question twenty times is inefficient for everyone involved.
You need to provide transcriptions or closed captions for your pre-recorded videos. Some students rely on reading the text to fully process the information.
Stop making quizzes that only allow you to view one question at a time without backtracking. It completely ruins our ability to manage our time and review our work.
Please stop using fonts like Comic Sans or Papyrus for official exams. It makes the test look like a middle school handout and undermines your authority.
You need to reply to discussion board posts occasionally. If the professor never chimes in, it just feels like the students are talking into a void.
Stop assigning group work for online asynchronous classes. It is nearly impossible to coordinate schedules with people we have never met across different time zones.
You need to be more understanding about technical issues. If the submission portal crashes at 11:58 PM, you shouldn't penalize students for being a minute late.
Please stop typing loudly on your mechanical keyboard without muting yourself on Zoom. The clacking sound completely drowns out the student who is trying to speak.
You need to invest in a better webcam. The 480p potato camera makes it impossible to see any physical props you try to hold up to the screen.
Stop using a virtual background that glitches constantly. It is incredibly distracting to watch parts of your head disappear into the generic beach photo.
You need to provide better lighting for your online lectures. Sitting in a dark room with a window behind you turns you into a silhouette. We can't see your face.
You need to actually read the drafts you make us submit. Returning a draft with zero comments makes the entire peer-review process feel like a waste of time.
Stop assigning essays without a page limit. "Write until you are finished" is terrifying. Give us a general ballpark so we know the scope of your expectations.
You need to give us more time for group discussions. Giving us sixty seconds to discuss a complex ethical dilemma is completely pointless.
Stop bringing your personal political views into a mathematics class. It is completely irrelevant to the subject matter and alienates half the room.
You need to be more mindful of the classroom temperature. If the room is freezing, please call maintenance. Nobody can focus on learning when they are shivering.
Stop testing us on obscure footnotes from the textbook. Focus your exams on the core concepts and major themes that you actually discussed in lecture.
Please stop using incredibly obscure vocabulary words when simple ones will do. You sound like a thesaurus, and it just confuses the international students.
You need to be consistent with your late policy. Accepting late work from some students but rigidly denying it to others is blatant favoritism.
Stop making attendance a graded component if you are just going to read the slides. We shouldn't be penalized for skipping a class that offers no extra value.
Stop standing directly in front of the projector. You are blocking the slides with your body, and the light is blinding you anyway. Stand to the side.
You need to calibrate your microphone properly. It is so loud that it physically hurts our ears when you raise your voice. Turn the gain down.
Stop giving exams that are entirely short-answer questions if you are only going to give us fifty minutes. We do not have the physical time to write that much.
You need to create a more welcoming environment for questions. When you sigh heavily every time a hand goes up, it trains the class to stay silent.
Please stop using dark blue text on a black background. It is an accessibility nightmare and completely illegible for anyone with visual impairments.
You need to communicate better with the disability resource center. Delaying a student's accommodations because you "forgot to check your email" is unacceptable.
Stop assuming everyone is a traditional student. Many of us work full-time jobs, and expecting us to attend a mandatory event on a Saturday is completely unreasonable.
You need to be more culturally sensitive. Some of the examples you use are highly outdated and rely on offensive stereotypes. Please update your material.
Stop relying on the textbook publisher's pre-made slides. They are generic, boring, and clearly not tailored to the specific way you want to teach the course.
Please stop talking over the students. When someone is trying to ask a question, let them finish their entire thought before you jump in to answer.
You need to check your links before class. Spending ten minutes trying to get a YouTube video to play wastes valuable instructional time.
You need to provide a clear timeline for the lecture. Giving us a brief agenda at the start of class helps us mentally prepare for the topics we will cover.
Stop comparing our class to your other sections. Telling us that your morning class is "so much smarter" is insulting and destroys our morale.
You need to learn the names of your students. Calling us "you in the blue shirt" in a class of only twenty people makes us feel completely anonymous and undervalued.
Please stop chewing gum while you lecture. The constant smacking noises are picked up by the microphone and it is incredibly distracting for the whole room.
You need to dress slightly more professionally. Showing up to lecture in sweatpants and a stained t-shirt makes it hard to take you seriously as an academic.
Your syllabus is far too rigid. If the whole class is failing to grasp a concept, you need to have the flexibility to spend an extra day on it, rather than rushing forward.
You need to actively moderate the discussion boards. When students post factually incorrect information, you need to step in and correct it before it spreads.
The way you structure the discussion boards is tedious. Forcing us to "reply to two peers" just results in everyone writing generic, meaningless comments.
Stop making the final project due on the very last day of classes. We have finals to study for. Move the deadline up a week so we can manage our time properly.
Your grading turnaround is unacceptable. If we take a quiz on Monday, we should have the grade by Friday, not three weeks later when the material is irrelevant.
You use far too many acronyms without writing them out. If you introduce a new abbreviation, write it clearly on the board so we aren't lost for the next hour.
You should implement a mid-semester feedback survey. You are completely blind to how much the class is struggling, and you need a way for us to tell you anonymously.
You need to be clearer about what is going to be on the final. "Everything we covered" is not a helpful study guide for a sixteen-week, content-heavy course.
Please stop looking at the clock every five minutes. It makes it seem like you hate being there, which completely kills the motivation of the students.
You need to stop pacing back and forth like a caged animal. It is incredibly distracting to watch and makes the entire front row feel dizzy.
The transitions between your slides are visually jarring and distracting. Stick to a simple cut rather than using wild spinning animations that give us headaches.
You provide zero opportunities for critical thinking. Everything is presented as absolute fact with no room for discussion, debate, or alternative perspectives.
Your teaching heavily favors rote memorization over actual comprehension. We can regurgitate the definitions, but none of us know how to apply them practically.
You need to provide a formula sheet. Memorizing thirty different complex statistical formulas is a waste of brain space. Test us on how to use them, not recall them.
The closed-book exams for an open-book subject make no sense. In the real world, we will have access to reference materials. Test our application, not memory.
Punishing sick students by forcing them to attend class to avoid losing points is reckless. You are creating a public health hazard in your own classroom.
Your attendance policy is archaic and unnecessarily strict. Dropping a letter grade for two absences doesn't account for real-life emergencies or illness.
The guest speakers you bring in are completely irrelevant to the course objectives. It feels like you are just trying to fill time rather than educate us.
There is a massive disconnect between the lecture and the lab. We are doing experiments on topics we won't cover in the main lecture for another three weeks.
Your TAs are entirely unhelpful during lab sessions. They sit on their phones instead of walking around to ensure we are setting up the equipment correctly.
You need to enforce safety protocols in the lab more strictly. Letting students walk around without goggles while handling chemicals is a massive liability.
The instructions for the labs are incredibly confusing. You need to rewrite the lab manuals to be clear, step-by-step guides rather than vague suggestions.
The reading load is completely unreasonable for a three-credit course. You need to curate the most important articles rather than assigning whole books every week.
The reading assignments do not align with the lectures at all. If you aren't going to discuss the chapters in class, don't make us read eighty pages a night.
The required software for this course is prohibitively expensive. You need to find free or open-source alternatives so low-income students aren't penalized.
Refusing to use Canvas makes the class unnecessarily confusing. We shouldn't have to navigate to your personal, poorly coded website just to find the syllabus.
If your laser pointer is broken, please replace it. Waving a dead piece of plastic at a screen doesn't help us identify which graph you are talking about.
The font size on your presentations is absurdly small. Use at least a 24-point font so the people who don't have perfect vision can actually read the material.
You erase the board far too quickly. Wait at least two minutes after you finish writing a complex equation before wiping it away. We are still copying it down.
You need to post your slides before class, not after. Having the slides in front of us allows us to take notes on what you say, rather than frantically copying text.
Do not delete the lecture recordings right before midterms. We rely on those to study and review complex topics. Leave them up for the entire semester.
Please stop refusing to record the lectures. Students get sick or have emergencies. Having a video archive is a basic accessibility feature you are denying us.
You cannot hold us past the scheduled end time. We have to walk across a massive campus to our next class. When the clock hits the hour, you must stop.
Always repeat a student's question into the microphone before answering it. The rest of the hall never hears what was asked, making your answer lack context.
You completely ignore the back half of the lecture hall. Make eye contact with the people sitting in the upper rows, not just the front three benches.
Stop letting the same one student dominate every discussion. You need to actively manage the classroom dynamics so quieter voices get a chance to be heard.
You have to learn how to handle awkward silences. Asking a question and staring at us for three minutes wastes time. If nobody answers, rephrase the question.
There is way too much group work in this class. We are paying to learn from your expertise, not to teach ourselves the material in breakout rooms.
You need to incorporate more small-group work. Sitting and listening for two hours is exhausting. Break us up to discuss the material and keep us engaged.
The aggressive cold-calling needs to stop immediately. It paralyzes students with anxiety and makes them dread coming to class instead of being excited to learn.
Your lectures are based on outdated theories. The field has moved on significantly in the last twenty years, and your curriculum needs to reflect those changes.
Refusing to answer "what if" questions stifles curiosity. Hypotheticals are how students test the boundaries of a theory, and you shouldn't dismiss them so quickly.
You desperately need visual aids. Explaining a complex biological process entirely through spoken word is ineffective for the visual learners in the room.
The material is incredibly dry. You need to find a way to inject some life into the curriculum, perhaps through case studies or interactive simulations.
You overcomplicate incredibly simple concepts. A good professor makes difficult things easy to grasp, but your explanations just add unnecessary layers of confusion.
Stop skipping the foundational steps. You jump straight to the advanced applications, leaving everyone who hasn't taken the prerequisites completely lost.
You use way too much industry jargon without defining it. Remember that we are beginners; you have to translate these concepts into plain English first.
The course is completely devoid of real-world examples. Connecting the abstract theories to current events would make the material so much easier to digest.
Stop treating this introductory class like a weed-out course. Your goal should be to help us understand the field, not to artificially fail half the roster.
You need to be more patient. Sighing heavily when a student asks you to repeat a concept shows a lack of empathy for the learning process.
Your sarcastic comments aren't as funny as you think they are. They often come across as mean-spirited and alienate the students you are directing them at.
You get incredibly defensive when someone points out a mistake on the slides. Just say thank you and fix it. We are all human, there's no need to argue.
Stop ghosting our emails. It shouldn't take a week and three follow-ups to get a simple "yes" or "no" answer regarding a homework extension.
Your email etiquette is frankly rude. Responding "read the syllabus" to a genuine clarifying question makes you seem completely uninvested in our success.
You have to actually attend your own office hours. I have shown up three times during the posted times, and your door has been locked every single time.
Your pop quizzes do nothing but cause extreme anxiety. They don't encourage studying; they just punish students who happen to have a bad morning.
The final exam shouldn't be worth 60% of our grade. That places an absurd amount of pressure on a single day and doesn't reflect our consistent effort.
You need to give partial credit for math problems. If a student understands the entire formula but makes one tiny addition error, they shouldn't get a zero.
Refusing to hand back our graded exams prevents us from learning from our mistakes. Let us see what we got wrong so we can study better for the final.
Review sessions need to actually be reviews. Just reading the syllabus again doesn't help. We need to work through practice problems together.
The multiple-choice options are unnecessarily confusing. When answers are "A and B, but not C, unless D," you are just creating artificial difficulty.
You cannot test us on chapters that you explicitly told us to skip. It destroys trust and artificially lowers our grades for no valid pedagogical reason.
Stop putting trick questions on the exams. Testing our ability to spot a double negative doesn't prove we understand the core concepts of the curriculum.
You deduct points for formatting errors but never provided a formatting guide. You cannot penalize students for failing to follow rules you never explicitly set.
Your instructions are wildly contradictory. The syllabus says one thing, the Canvas page says another, and you say a third thing in class. Please get on the same page.
The amount of busywork in this course is staggering. Please cut down on the daily reading quizzes and focus on a few meaningful, deep-learning assignments.
Stop playing favorites. It is painfully obvious that you grade the students who speak up in class more leniently than the quiet ones. Grade blindly to ensure fairness.
The grading curve is incredibly punishing. If the class average is a 40%, the problem is your teaching style and test design, not the students' intelligence.
Your grading rubrics are way too vague. "Show good effort" is not a measurable metric. We need clear, specific guidelines on how to achieve full marks.
Please erase the board completely before starting a new problem. Writing new equations over the faint ghosts of old equations makes everything an illegible mess.
Your handwriting is beautiful but far too small. Anyone sitting past the middle of the lecture hall has no chance of reading the formulas you write out.
You need to actually write things down. Verbally listing six complex steps without writing them on the board guarantees that half the class will get them wrong.
The monotone voice makes the 8 AM lecture unbearable. Please try to add some inflection and energy to your delivery so we can stay awake and engaged.
Try to avoid going on so many tangents. We spend half the class talking about your weekend or random news events instead of the material we will be tested on.
You need to incorporate pauses. You speak so fast that nobody can take accurate notes. Give us a few seconds to process the information before jumping to the next topic.
Your pacing is incredibly erratic. You rush through the complex theories in five minutes and then spend half an hour on a simple introductory anecdote.
You speak entirely too softly. Even sitting in the second row, I have to strain to hear you. You absolutely must project your voice or wear a microphone.
Stop using a laser pointer on the TV screen; we can't see it on the lecture capture recordings. Use the digital mouse pointer so online students can follow along.
Please mute students who have background noise on Zoom. The constant dog barking and typing sounds make it impossible to focus on the lecture material.
You rely way too heavily on YouTube videos to do your teaching for you. We pay tuition to learn from a professor, not to watch a playlist we could have found ourselves.
If you are going to teach online, you need to look at the camera. Staring off-screen the entire time makes it feel incredibly disconnected and impersonal.
The course software you force us to use is buggy and outdated. Please switch to a more modern platform that doesn't crash every time we try to take a quiz.
Your announcements are always sent out at the last minute. We need more than a few hours' notice if a class is being moved to Zoom or canceled.
Stop locking the homework dropboxes right at 11:59 PM without a grace period. A one-minute delay shouldn't result in a zero for a heavily weighted essay.
Organize the learning modules better. Everything is dumped into one giant folder, and students waste hours just trying to find the right presentation.
You need to update your syllabus. The dates are from three years ago, and we are constantly guessing when our actual assignments are due.
Please fix the broken links on the course page. Half of the assigned reading materials lead to error pages, making it impossible to complete the homework on time.
We paid a ridiculous amount for the textbook, yet you never once reference it or assign readings from it. Either integrate the book into your teaching style or don't require it at all.
You should be more open to debate. The moment a student offers an alternative interpretation of the text, you shut them down. College is about exploring ideas, not just parroting your views.
Your communication skills are lacking. If a student emails you a question, you need to respond within a reasonable timeframe. Ignoring student emails completely is unacceptable.
You really need to learn how to moderate a class discussion. Right now, you just let the loudest, most obnoxious students dominate the room while the rest of us sit in absolute silence.
You get so bogged down in the microscopic details that we lose the big picture. Every once in a while, you need to zoom out and remind us how all these tiny facts fit into the main theory.
Relying this heavily on videos and guest speakers makes it seem like you don't want to teach. Use them sparingly as a supplement, but you need to actually lead the instruction yourself.
The transitions between subjects are jarring. You jump from Chapter three to Chapter seven without explaining the connection. You need to build a clearer bridge between the different concepts.
Try connecting the material back to our actual major. This is a required course, but you treat it like an isolated bubble. Show us why this subject matters for our future careers.
You have to stop changing the due dates randomly without sending out an announcement. It is infuriating to plan out a study schedule only to find out the essay was moved up by two days.
They just sit there. You should have them walking around helping students during practice problems.
The aggressive cold-calling creates a terrifying classroom environment. It doesn't make us learn better; it just makes us incredibly anxious. Please switch to a volunteer-based system.
You rely exclusively on talking, but some of us are visual learners. You need to incorporate more diagrams, charts, and videos into your teaching style to accommodate everyone.
Stop putting trick questions on the exams. A test should measure our understanding of the material, not our ability to navigate your linguistic traps and intentionally confusing wording.
You need to enforce your rules evenly.
The homework load is completely unreasonable and mostly consists of busywork. Cut out the repetitive, pointless assignments and give us meaningful work that actually reinforces learning.
You clearly play favorites in discussions, only calling on the same three people. A good professor involves the whole class and makes everyone feel like their input is valued.
Stop drowning us in academic jargon. You throw around complex terminology without ever defining it first. Break the concepts down into plain English before throwing in the fancy words.
It would help so much if you took the last two minutes of class to summarize the main takeaways. Right now, lectures just abruptly end and we are left wondering what the core point was.
You spend forty minutes on the easiest chapter and then cram the most difficult, math-heavy chapter into the last ten minutes. You seriously need to balance your time management better.
Being a notoriously harsh grader doesn't make you a better professor, especially when you don't leave feedback. If you are going to take off points, you have to explain exactly why.
You need to actually be present and helpful during office hours. Every time I go, you seem annoyed that I'm there. Office hours are supposed to be for helping struggling students.
The lectures lack a clear structure. You just ramble from point to point without any logical flow. An outline at the start of class would drastically improve comprehension.
Please pause occasionally so we can catch up on our notes. You click to the next slide before anyone has even finished reading the first bullet point. It's beyond frustrating.
The material needs a serious update. Using examples and software from a decade ago is unacceptable in a fast-moving field. You have to modernize your lectures to make them relevant.
You need to reevaluate how you handle group projects. Forcing group work without any peer evaluation means the slackers get a free ride while one person does all the heavy lifting.
The assignment prompts are incredibly vague. We shouldn't have to guess what you want. Please write clear, detailed instructions so we can actually focus on the work itself.
You have to stop holding us past the bell. We have other classes to get to across campus. When time is up, you need to wrap up the lecture, not start a brand new slide.
Please respect our time and start class on schedule. Consistently showing up ten minutes late throws off the whole morning and makes it feel like you don't care about the course.
You need to be more open to being wrong. Getting defensive and snapping at students who point out a math error on the board creates a really toxic classroom environment.
You have a bad habit of overcomplicating very simple concepts. A good teacher makes hard things easy to understand, but you somehow make easy things feel impossible to comprehend.
Talking at us for ninety minutes is an outdated teaching method. You really need to incorporate some interactive elements, discussions, or active learning so we don't just zone out.
The exams need to actually align with the lectures. Right now, it feels like we are being tested on a completely different class. Stop using test banks and write your own relevant questions.
Returning grades faster is essential. Getting our midterm feedback two weeks before the final exam doesn't give us any time to correct our mistakes and improve our study habits.
The Canvas page is an absolute labyrinth. Please reorganize it logically by week or module. Students shouldn't have to spend twenty minutes clicking around just to find the homework drop box.
The pacing is agonizingly slow. We spend way too much time on simple concepts that everyone grasps immediately. You need to read the room and move on when we clearly get it.
Stop assuming everyone already knows the basics. This is an intro class, but you teach it like a master's seminar. You have to build the foundation before diving into the complex math.
You need to work on being more approachable. Your demeanor is so intimidating that nobody wants to raise their hand when they don't understand something. It's hurting our learning.
A little enthusiasm would help. The monotone delivery puts the entire lecture hall to sleep. Varying your vocal pitch would make the material significantly more engaging.
The personal stories are sometimes funny, but you go on so many tangents that we never finish the lesson plan. You need to stay on track so we actually cover the exam material.
A rubric would go a long way. The grading feels entirely arbitrary. If you want us to succeed, you have to clearly communicate what you actually expect from our assignments.
The course structure is a mess. You need a more organized syllabus. Jumping between topics randomly makes it impossible to know what we should be preparing for each week.
Whenever a student asks a question, the professor dances around it instead of giving a direct answer. It would help immensely if you actually addressed the core of what we are confused about.
The theory is great, but it would be much more effective if you tied it to real-world examples. Without practical applications, the concepts are just floating in the void and hard to grasp.
Please stop just reading the PowerPoint slides word for word. We can read them ourselves at home. The lectures need to add actual value and deeper explanation to be worth attending.

reviews.comment: Lecture attendance is not necessary at all as he records and uploads all of them. Some people here are saying he's rude when in reality I would just say he's blunter than people are used to but nothing excessive. He's very accommodating for late homework and exam rescheduling. I wouldn't say he's my favorite professor, but he's very fair.
wow tough guy
You do not need to attend his lecture and you can learn it well by yourself. Does not care his students and very rude and mean to everyone for no reason.
He is just very unprepared and rude. Does not respond to emails well at all.

I truly do not recommend this professor, as he treats students with a lack of courtesy and always speaks to them in a condescending manner. He responds to emails slowly and has a poor attitude. Additionally, he enjoys nitpicking and tends to make a big deal out of small issues.
There is absolutely no need to attend his lecture

Bi's lectures were very scattered and he would skip over material often. He is pretty generous about giving students a lot of time for assignments which was nice. He was, however, condescending to students during the research project for this class, and very nit-picky.

He is a totally tough grader. He will take points off even if it is a very trivial point. For example, he will take points off if you don't use an appropriate word out of a 12 pages project report. Also, he doesn't reply to emails on time.
Bi is a wonderful professor. I've learned a lot about R code and stats. My one thing is that it's kinda hard to study for in-person exams.

Instructor Wu is not capable to explain things well. The logic of the lecture is unclear, and he is fond of skipping materials. If you ask him to explain anything more in detail, he will just tell you that you are not required to know it. He doesn't care about any academic dishonesty, but he always feels extremely satisfied with himself.

Didn't really pay attention to lecture and just read the notes provided and got a A in the class. Overall, Professor Wu knows and teaches the content well, but gets through it FAR too slowly, making the class incredibly boring. The homeworks also take several hours to complete each week as well.

Took Professor Bi for Stat 240 and it was a great first introduction to programming in R and statistics in general. In lectures he does live coding demos, so you can try to follow along with him or just read along in the notes. Compared to current Professor I have for stat 340, I would choose Bi 100/100 times.

I was genuinely surprised by the quality of his lectures. Heard the class was hard but he made everything super clear and went over every detail. Ecen though its a stats class the most important part is understanding the conceptual stuff well. If you can analyze the details of a scenario and relate them to the different equations then it is easy.

Bi was a breath of fresh air after dealing with the Math department for the last two years! He always responded to student questions and made learning stats easy. I appreciate how in depth he went into the material to make sure it was easy to understand. Bi allowed notes and R (stats programming language) on tests which helped a ton. Great class.
reviews.rating_tags: Lots of homework--Accessible outside class--Online Savvy

reviews.comment: not good

Bi himself is very caring and understanding. He is very lenient towards late work and is very accommodating to any students who run into issues while taking his course. The one problem with Bi is that there were very few projects and homework-so while you might think it is a good thing, it makes studying for exams and being prepared very difficult.
reviews.rating_tags: Test heavy--Graded by few things--Accessible outside class

reviews.comment: Lectures are all recorded and are well organized and focus heavily on live coding demos but cover general concepts well too. All graded work is take-home/open note, but it all takes a long time. Just stay on top of the content and be prepared to spend a lot of time on homework and you'll be fine.
I like his vibe, smart and sharp. He is also super kind and passionate about teaching. A very responsible professor!
Prof. Zhang knows the materials well. He genuinely cares about the students, and is very approachable.

This is the course that I learned the most in the past two years. It actually taught the skills that I later applied during the summer intern. Dayin is a very thoughtful professor, that cares about the students.
reviews.rating_tags: Amazing lectures --Clear grading criteria--Gives good feedback

reviews.comment: Professor Zhang is an outstanding educator. He actively engages the class by posing thoughtful questions and continuously refines the course throughout the semester to better meet students' needs. This ability to adapt responsively is, in my view, a rare and commendable quality among professors.

Dayin is a nice guy and a well-respected researcher in the real estate world. However, for this course, I found the lectures unengaging, the course material poorly taught, and the grading structure did not make any sense. I would recommend taking this course with a different professor.

Very boring, hard to understand lectures. Some things would be graded absurdly easy (wrong answers get full credit on one exam) but then other things like the case assignment get graded incredibly harsh based off things he never outlined in the rubric for us to cover. This class convinced me to change my major, just a bad experience all around.

Dayin is a fine teacher when presenting lectures, but his exams and homeworks were the issue. They are a bit lengthy, but most prevalently they were often confusing. Most were 3 long questions and each time 1/3 would be things that were a large jump from what we covered in class. Material is a bit confusing, but stay on top of it and you'll be ok.

Dan is great. I am majoring in entom so I might be biased, but I think even if you aren't into insects this class is really interesting and fun bc he just knows so many fun little facts. You can tell he really cares.

Dr. Young was a great professor! He's a funny old beetle taxonomist. I took his FIG course, and he was really enjoyable. You do have to read quite a bit of material, but if you find biodiversity interesting it isn't that bad. Just know that he doesn't use canvas, and instead only emails. Overall though, he made my first semester a good one!
reviews.rating_tags: Get ready to read--Respected--Graded by few things

reviews.comment: Dr Young is easily the best professor I've had during my time at UW, really funny guy and really passionate about the topic.  The content isn't particularly easy but it is taught enthusiastically so it makes it easier to learn and actually understand.

Dan is probably my favorite professor I've ever had. I did his FIG freshman year and then took this class so that I could have him as a prof again. So funny, and really cares about getting his students just as excited as he is about insects. This class is definitely a lot of work -- but Dan does a great job of helping you through everything.

Dan is the best professor I met ever! 
In entomology, he was able to expertly answer every tricky question asked by students. Dan is so professional to identify every insects of my collection in few seconds. 
During the lectures, Dan helped students understand obscure and difficult points in a fun and clear way while ensuring professionalism.

Dan Young is the best professor I have ever had at UW, I cant put it into words how much I love and appreciate this man and the wonder he instills in me over insects. He has inspired me to major in entomology and I found the collection to be the most fun part of the course. Lab exams can be a pain sometimes but the field work is very fun 11/10
Super fun and engaging professor!
Incredibly dense course with lots of exams but Dan makes it genuinely interesting to learn. Extremely chill professor who will joke around a lot. Get ahead on the collection early, trust me.

One of the best if not the best professor I've ever met. His teaching style is quite laid back but does well to simplify concepts and create analogies that allows easier understanding and stimulate interest. He is very chill and one of the most engaging too, his star trek referrences and other jokes throughout lectures and labs are really fun.

Dan is genuinely the best professor I have ever had! I was a student of his in four different courses that he taught and loved every single one. He is one of the most caring and passionate professor I had throughout college. Dan left such a big impact on me and really made me enjoy learning again. I genuinely cant thank him enough for all his help.
I would absolutely take his class again. He is so passionate about what he is teaching and makes a large effort to engage his students in his content. He is a great person and also quite funny.

This class is super interesting, but get ready to dedicate your whole life to it. Dan goes through material very quickly and there was so much taxonomy to cover. Outside of having class, the collections project took up every weekend. He's very charismatic and tries to use analogies to make concepts make sense, but it can end up being more confusing

Dan is an amazing professor. Took the FIG and his was easily my favorite class this semester. Cares about each of his students, jokes around, and you can tell he's really passionate about these things. The readings were kind of a lot but he's a forgiving grader. Will be taking 302 so I can have him again.
Good Teacher. His quizzes are tough but his exams are good. Do well on exams study for quizzes and do well on the project and you'll be fine.

This class makes me wish I could take more entom. classes, especially with Dan as the prof! This class left me with a new way of viewing nature & insects. Very demanding class though. As soon as you get your kill jar, force yourself to go collecting at least every weekend, and get classmates' contact info to trade with. Make Quizlets to study!

This class was very stressful at times (7 total exams + insect collection) but it was one of the most rewarding classes I've taken. Dan can come off as somewhat strict, but he's actually very forgiving (gave extra credit when an exam score was low). His lectures made me wanna read about insects in my free time! I have no complaints about Dan

This discussion class is fairly simple. Take notes of required weekly readings and send discussion questions back to him via email for the next class. With several weeks left, readings end and biodiversity hotspot presentations and essays are assigned. Roughly follow the rubric and put in some effort for an A, which most people get.

He and I had a roller coaster of a semester but roller coasters are exciting. The material was SO interesting and he knows his stuff. He is a really wonderful STEM professor who knows who you are and really is on your side. Entomology is one of my favorite classes here and I recommend it. IT IS TOUGH.. but Dan gives you the resources to succeed.

Professor Young is one of the best professors that I've had in my college career. He is caring, hilarious, and very passionate about what he teaches and researches. He is an incredible man and I would definitely take a course with him again.

An awesome guy but the bug project was a lot of work. Took 20+ hours. There were 7 exams in total between what he basically assumed was a separate lab and lecture though they are 4 credits together. Would not recommend this class for someone who was just interested in insects and isn't dedicated to a future to them.
This class is so much fun. The project was great and it helped boost my great. I never knew how important insects were before taking his class.
Best 300 class I have ever taken.
His lab was the easiedt lab that I have ever taken. The bug project was fun.
This is an amazing class to get a head start on insects. You really understand their why they all matter and how they are related. He also tells us that insects have feelings too.
He is an awesome professor his love insects makes him so happy to help his students.
He is my favorite professor ever. He gave the best lectures along with the best labs I had ever taken. I loved his exams.
He taught the class in a way students could understand it and he had some of the best tests than most bio teachers here.
I loved his labs and project his test were well written with good answers you can remember from class.
Start on bug collection early (note time and place as well). Great professor but both lecture and lab exams every few weeks.

Dr. Young was one of my favorite professors I've ever had (I'm a fourth year), however this class was also one of the hardest I've taken at Madison. Make sure you go to EVERY lecture. Even though he provides online notes which are very helpful, it is important to go because he goes over much more in class. Also study for lab exams!
reviews.rating_tags: Tough Grader--Respected--Skip class? You won't pass.

reviews.comment: This is by far the most rewarding class that I've ever taken at UW-Madison. If you are at all interested in insects, I cannot recommend it enough. Dr. Young's enthusiasm for the subject is contagious and he does a great job of explaining the material. As long as you are willing to put in the work, Entomology 302 isn't too difficult.

One of the most inspiring classes I've taken. He sends out all his lectures but goes through them pretty fast. It's best to print them all out beforehand.  I found it hard to get a hold of him outside of class, even though he says he's always in his office. He and the course has definitely changed my outlook on insects.
I LOVE DAN!!!! The best professor I've had at UW-Madison. He's compelling and funny and very into what he's teaching. He tells you everything you need to know for the exams you just have to listen.
Professor is good but this is the Worst course project and course design I've ever had as a senior....
VERY nice professor. LOVED him...The class is not extraordinarily hard, but very time-consuming and you need to do a lot of memorization. Take it if you are super interested in bugs!

Probably the best professor i have ever had at UW. Extremely enthusiastic and loves the subject. Really made me excited and made the class very enjoyable. I would highly recommend that everyone take this class if they can.

Overall, Dr. Young was the most enthusiastic professor I have seen on this campus! I would recommend taking this course in Fall and START COLLECTING BUGS EARLY (the second you register for this class).  Kill bugs in 70% Ethanol. Flashcards work great for studying. Schedule extra time in the lab weekly for reviewing material and you should be fine!

Class is way more difficult than anticipated. I also do not see what is so great about this guy. I thought this class was very dry, as bugs would be. Unless you have a burning desire to learn about bugs, don't take it. Worst decision i've made at the uw.

Dr. Young is the best professor I have ever taken. He is smart, funny, and best of all, makes you want to learn and appreciate insects that surround us everyday. The course is DEMANDING so dont procrastinate. He has no sympathy for students who do bad in the course or those who dont finish their projects on time!

Hands down the best professor I've ever had! He's funny and insightful. I was so worried about the class but once in it, it was a blast! Get to know him on a personal level and you will ace. There is a lot of time required for the insect collection, so start RIGHT AWAY. Go to ALL his reviews and for the lab exams, spend a lot of time in the lab.

Best professor ever. This class inexplicably made me want to spend my weekends memorizing the latin names of beetle families. Now, I notice bugs wherever I go. It's kind of a neat party trick to identify the bug in the room, and has come in surprisingly useful at my job, in other classes, and in my personal life.
DAN YOUNG IS the best prof on campus.  seriously...take any class he offers.  most passionate man on campus
He was interesting, helpful, fair, and challenging. Ties with a couple others for best professor I've had at UW-Madison.
One of the best classes that I have taken. It was work, but Dan made it fun and interesting. Lectures were always entertaining and tests were fair

Professor Young is the best! I was terrified of bugs but with a lot of flashcards and his awesome lectures, I was able to easily get an A and now know SO MUCH about insects. Get to know the material AND the professor--both very interesting! And don't procrastinate on your collection of 75 different specimens...it's no joke. Highly recommended!!!

Great professor and made the course material interesting even though at first glance it may not seem to be so.  The class is 4 credits, but should probably be bumped up to 5 due to the amount of time spent in the lab.  Tests were fair.  Insect collection requires a lot of time.  Take class in the fall and start collecting in the summer!

Dan Young will make you love bugs if you have hated them your entire life. It is a lot of work but his reviews are helpful and he basically tells you question by question what will be on the exam, you just need to study that material. Flashcards were helpful, especially the ones you can make online because there's a lot. Overall, loved him!

Dr. Young is awesome! Very funny, and tells great anecdotes to help you learn the information. NOT an easy class though-there are a ton of terms to memorize. Flash cards are necessary, and it's a lot of work. If you have any interest in insects, you'll learn tons of fascinating stuff! I took this class for fun, and wasn't disappointed.
I love Prof Young. He's knowledgeable, helpful, and will do whatever he can to help you understand the material. He also clearly loves insects and his enthusiasm is contagious.
Prof Young knocked my socks off!
absolutely fantastic. never thought I would be so interested in insects. Totally due to dr. young.

You NEED to take this class if it counts toward your major.  It's very dense with material, but is extremely easy to remember if you attend lecture because Professor Young explains everything in a humorous, totally relatable way.  He is, for lack of a better word, AMAZING.  Going in I was apathetic toward insects; coming out I was enthusiastic.

This guy could make dirt interesting. Now that aside, the class is very information heavy, lots of memorizing and lab time. Plus a big bug collection, but go on the field trips and trade with others and its not a problem. Don't let all that scare you, this class was one of the best classes I've taken on campus, and mainly because of Prof Young.

Professor Young is amazing.  You will serious not regret one second taking this class.  Much, much better than all the other zoology classes I've taken - he reminded me why I'm passionate about animals.

Professor Young is one of those professors with a distinct passion for what they do. He is engaging, funny, and becuase he runs lecture, lab and feild trips, you get plenty of interaction with him. Class material does invovle alot of memorization, and his lab and lecture books are a little jumbled, but Young was a great professor and made up for it

AMAZING PROFESSOR.  If only all professors had his exact teaching style.  The man is HILARIOUS, repeats things so many times studying is not too big of a hassle (as long as you pay attention), runs all lectures, labs, and field trips and wears sweatpants and a bug shirt every day.  I hated bugs but he made them interesting.

i feel the need to share a quote, just to demonstrate his sense of humor: we were talking about scorpionflies in lecture, which have a copulatory organ on one end which makes them look like, obiously, scorpions. Dan told us that if you catch one they'll whip it around at you like they sting, but don't worry, they can only **** you a little bit.

This class is hard. It's really hard. There's lots of memorization, frequent tests, and the collection will take quite a bit of work. But that DOESN'T MATTER because prof Young is AMAZING. This class was what I dreamed college would be like. Lectures are fascinating, you learn a ton. Absolutely the best class I've taken. Take it!

Best professor i have had at UW. Extremely helpful, will answer any question clearly. Very funny and personable also. Makes the material extremely interesting. He really wants you to do well in the class. If you take his class you wont be disappointed, but DO NOT procrastinate on the collection!

If you're considering taking this class, take it with Dr. Young. His lectures are entertaining and bawdy, he has an incredible passion for the material, and he obviously loves teaching. Lots of memorization and insect collecting is required, but it's worth it for the man.

BEST PROFESSOR I'VE EVER HAD! he teaches in such a way that you just can't help but learn the stuff really well. it makes studying so much easier! he makes bugs really interesting, which is a really hard thing to do. take this class!

I could not imagine a better professor! This guy is hilarious. If you need a zoology class or plan on becoming an Ent major take his intro course (ent 302). You will not be disappointed! He has a weekly "entomological moment in middle-earth" up on the lab board...if that gives you any clue what kind of guy you'd be dealing with.

He is THE best professor that I have had/ probably ever will have.  Lectures are entertaining and he is just a cool guy overall.  If all my professors were like him going to classes would be so much easier.

Who knew that lectures about bugs could be so entertaining? Not only is this man hilarious, but he knows pretty much everything about insects. The best part of the class: no TAs, he does the lectures, labs, and field trips all himself. Very quick to grade and return things too. He acts very casual and is always reasonable. Highly recomended.
Loved Him!!  Expected to hate the class.  Put off taking this required class because I hated bugs.  Now I collect them and would have changed majors if I'd had the time.  He's THAT good.
He's fantastic!
No Comments
One of the best teachers I've ever had

Math 211. Delong is awesome! He explains the material simply and clearly. Office hours are a few times a week and he is always available. Attendance isn't mandatory.. but helpful. Video recordings of the lectures are posted after class time. Super nice person and passionate about what he does.
Excellent and humorous teacher.

The lectures were very informative and clear with many examples. The homework/discussion packets were much more difficult than any material we were actually tested on. Prof D was very kind and I would definitely recommend him!
Very good lecturer. Math 234 is a fairly easy class until the last third of the semester, where it ramps up quite a bit. Make sure you understand earlier material so that you don't fail the final.

As a Calculus 3 course, Math 234 is quite challenging. The homework and worksheets of the discussion session may be relatively difficult, but the exams and quizzes are easier than those. Additionally, after class, professor Matt Delong posts all course slides on canvas, which is beneficial for students who prefer self-study.
reviews.rating_tags: Amazing lectures --Clear grading criteria--Lots of homework

reviews.comment: Although class was very difficult, it was easy to tell that Prof DeLong cares about his students and wants them to succeed and understand the concepts. Some concepts were not explained enough, but I always felt decently prepared for exams. Homework was much more difficult than exams or quizzes.

Though the class content is very difficult, Matt is such a caring and funny professor! He does a great job using analogies to simplify complicated concepts. Attendance is not required but he puts an emphasis on how important participation is. The class is a little homework heavy (~3 weekly assignments + 1 quiz) but definitely doable.
Prof DeLong is kind and humorous! Best Maths teacher I've ever met!

He is a kind and caring professor. However, his exam style made the course much harder than expected. Unlike other calculus exams, his tests were heavily multiple-choice and focused more on conceptual thinking than past exams. Since exams made up about 87% of the grade, this format change made it difficult for me to prepare and perform well.

There were part of the class where he rushed through complicated concepts, however by the last unit his examples and analogies were very helpful. It was very helpful that his lectures were posted online and you can tell he cares about his students

Dr. Delong cares a lot about his students! He would always try to explain difficult concepts by dumbing it down (making really good analogies), however he would sometimes go a bit fast and I wouldn't understand it, but watching the lecture after helped.

Absolutely lovely person. He made a point before every class to go around the hall and talk to a few people. He always kept up good energy throughout lecture that made it easier to pay attention. He prioritizes you as a person rather than a student. 234 is pretty tough compared to 221 and 222, so make sure to go to class and practice

Overall a very good professor, nothing stands out as amazing, but nothing stands out as a flaw either. Lectures were recorded, were usually easy to follow, with time well spent discussing new topics and going through examples. Occasionally topics at the end of lecture were rushed, but I would absolutely take another class taught by Prof. Delong.

Prof. Delong was my first math professor for college and he definitely set the bar high. Engaging lectures, does a good job trying to simplify hard concepts, and he is a very caring and considerate person. The nature of the class is test heavy and lots of content, but that is not him personally. Definitely take a class with him if you can!
Amazing amazing professor! Really cares about his students' understanding and his teaching is fun and straight-forward.

Professor Delong is a great math professor, it was his first semester teaching at a big school when I had him, but I wouldn't have known that if he hadn't told us. He does a wonderful job of explaining material and is extremely knowledgeable in the topics he teaches.

While he is not a bad professor, his lectures are difficult to sit through, and he always rushes through the material without much depth in his explanations. He will provide practice problems in class; however, they are done before the concept has been fully explained, making them hard to complete. Most of my learning was done independently of him.
reviews.rating_tags: Lecture heavy--Test heavy--Graded by few things

reviews.comment: Dr. Delong is the best math instructor I have ever had. He presents tough concepts in an extremely understandable and clear way. He uses a microphone and top hat questions to keep students engaged and involved in lecture. He is super funny and kind, and I can tell he cares a ton about our learning. If you take 234 at UW, make sure you get him!

Professor wasn't great at explaining things but he was always willing to sit down with you and explain it over and over. Exams are literally just the slides and what he says in lecture. If you attend lecture and discussion and pay attention you should do just fine. Everyone who went consistently did well on the exams. Labs + Quizzes are free points

Not great. He is clearly very knowledgeable and extremely intelligent, but the lecture slides were a mess, and since tests were purely based off of those it made studying extremely tedious and frustrating. 

Hoping the WSB changes this course structure entirely very soon, but for now I'd avoid.
avoid remi at all costs.
reviews.rating_tags: Tough grader--Test heavy--Graded by few things

reviews.comment: genuinely worst professor ever. the only two positive reviews on here were obviously written by him. Im either going to get an AB or an A, but regardless, NEVER TAKE A CLASS WITH REMI DAVIET

Remi is hands down the worst professor I have had at UW-Madison. His lecture slides are horribly written, he is practically impossible to reach the moment lecture is over, he doesn't give any practice material,TAs don't even know whats going on, and he tries to teach PhD-level material. My only word of advice is to never take a class with Remi.

Professor Remi is so nice and is one of my favourite professors. I don't understand why the ppl below are talking irrationally and with bias. You should be responsible for your low score if you don't show up to class. Professor Remi is very knowledgeable and has a sense of humor, he actually makes tedious stuff more interesting. 100% recommend.

He was a great professor that really cared for those of us that bothered to show up. (lecture/discussion attendance were abysmal) Everyone that went to discussion and lecture thought the exams were easy
He would give us information on the job market and made it clear through actions he wanted us to succeed
Extremely knowledgeable and fun to talk to

Remi isn't available outside of class, as he doesn't offer office hours. He just reads directly off the slide and provides no further context. Even the TAs agree that he overcomplicates the material, and the TAs told me that they do not understand the material themselves, since it's Phd level material. Worst professor in the entire bschool

Gen bus 307 is the worst class I have taken at Madison and it's not even close. I don't even know what this class is supposed to teach you and remi makes it so tedious for no reason. The activities in this class are super easy, but the exams, hell no. The averages are so low and the grade cutoffs are not in your favor so he def gonna have to curve.
reviews.rating_tags: Tough grader--Lecture heavy--Graded by few things

reviews.comment: Professor Daviet is horrible, avoid him if you can. He wants to make everything unnecessary difficult for no reason.

Such a free elective. 1 50 min. lecture a week with a discussion. Attendance for both are a big part of the grade, but if you have half a brain you will pass with an A. Each week you watch either an in person play (5 total) or an online one. During discussion you take a quiz asking easy questions about the play which are straight forward if watched
This professor was really understanding, and there are many extra credit opportunities that give you a lot of points. You'll get an A as long as you do the work.

Super chill professor. His class was a nice way to take a break from more intensive classes and actually be interested/entertained. Many extra credit opportunities and few assignments. He also has a generous grades policy If you don't miss lecture or any assignments for the first two months, you can just stop doing the class and get an A.

Dan is a super nice guy and his lectures are super easy. Although lectures are mandatory, the content is easy to digest and the weekly responses are super easy. This is a very easy A as long as you do the assignments and see the shows.

This class was super low stress and super easy. Attendance for lecture is mandatory but lecture content is not super important. Biggest portion of your grade is attending/watching performances and submitting reactions and responses to other classmates. Make-up assignments are offered but not always free. Overall, easy class and GPA booster.
Decent lecturer but the class is a surefire A if you just show up.

I loved this professor. And as long as you complete all of the work, you should definitely be able to receive the grade that you want. Furthermore, he is very understanding, and you can tell that he wants you to succeed. I enjoyed going to this class, and I would take it again and recommend it to others! This professor was overall great.

As long as you did assignments on time and show up to lecture an A was guaranteed. Took the Comm B portion and LOVED it. Would recommend to everyone and anyone. Nicest, coolest, and kindest professor around.

Cool Class! Consisted of watching theatrical productions both live and recorded, and interviewing various theatre professionals from within and outside of the university. 2 credit section graded only on discussion posts about the interviews and productions, and daily attendance. Only 1 Comm B section offered alongside the large 2 credit lecture.

She has a true talent for teaching Philosophy! Class is a large discussion, each week there is a short modern reading and we spend lecture talking with neighbors and giving our ideas to her. She asks questions which naturally lead the discussion to the point she wants to make. Much more engaging than the other 101 profs. You will make many friends!

Dani has been wonderful! I was a bit wary at the beginning of the semester, since her lectures are very discussion-based, but now, I look forward to going to her class each week. She really cares about each individual in her class and makes sure that everyone's perspectives are heard. There is a very light workload. Participation is crucial!

The topics that were discussed weren't super engaging and conversations were repetitive, we would spend multiple lectures talking about the same things. It seemed like she called on the same few people for every class discussion, so we weren't getting diverse perspectives. The QCCRs which were the main assignments for the class felt forced.

There isn't too much work for the class. Shemade us lead discussions but, a lot of times there was one specific point she would want us to hit however she wouldn't lead us there. It got to the point that we would repeat the same things about the lesson over and over. The same people ran the class, and she definitely had favorites.

This class was structured differently than all of my other classes. She is a very approachable human being and cares most about the success of everyone. Attending lecture is a very important chunk of the grade as well as only a few assignments and readings. Overall, a great teacher to help introduce the subject of philosophy.

Professor Clevenger was super nice, and you could tell she cared about her students. She broke big ideas down into bite-sized pieces and took time to make sure everyone understood. Lots of participation and active learning, and most of the lectures are discussion based.

Dr. Marin-Spiotta is a great lecturer. Her lessons go by quick and she's thorough in everything she teaches. The discussions are pretty good too, I had a great TA this semester. However, I struggle to understand the point of the writing assignments we had to do this semester, as they didn't prepare us for the actual material at all.

This is one of the "easier" science courses to take however thats the biggest lie ever. We had 4 exams including one 2 days after we came back from Spring Break. The professor is boring, nobody attends lecture and are either on their phones. Not to mention the amount of work assigned in discussion, its never that serious its a class about rocks lol

Tests were based off lectures (recorded/no attendence) but still omg this class is so bad. So much busy work, weekly writing assignments, worksheets, and quizzes. My TA has not come to half of the discussion sections and literally knows nothing. everyone is in a constant state of confusion and communication is lacking between prof TA and students.

Spiotta is fantastic. I enjoyed lecture and always learned something new. Supportive of students and their question. There is a final paper due at the end, but the criteria and ability to choose your topic makes it enjoyable. Great feedback from Professor & TA on assignment and essay submissions.
